description: Proscenium, thrust, in-the-round, traverse and promenade: how the space shapes the audience.
content_html:
The Stage Configuration Question

Before any set is built, any costume is made, or any performer begins rehearsing, a director and designer make a foundational choice: where will the audience sit relative to the performance? This is the performer-audience configuration. It shapes every other decision. A gobo that projects a crisp image in a proscenium theatre becomes irrelevant when the audience sits on three sides. A piece of blocking that puts a performer’s back to the audience is a problem in end-on staging but a routine occurrence in theatre in the round. You need to understand each configuration, its advantages, its limitations, and what it demands of performers and designers.

Key Fact

The six staging configurations are: proscenium arch, thrust stage, theatre in the round, traverse, end-on staging, and promenade. Each creates a different relationship between performer and audience. The configuration a director chooses is itself an interpretive statement about what they want that relationship to feel like.

Proscenium Arch

In a proscenium arch theatre, the arch is a picture frame. The audience sees only one face of the stage. This configuration supports illusionistic staging — elaborate sets, painted backdrops, hidden machinery — because the wings (the offstage areas to either side) are invisible to the audience. Designers can make use of upstage depth to create pictorial compositions, with performers positioned across the width of the stage in what is called a stage picture. The further a performer moves upstage, the smaller and less dominant they appear; moving downstage increases their size, presence and power over the audience’s attention.

The limitation of the proscenium is distance and the fourth wall. The audience is a unified mass of observers watching events they are not part of. Naturalistic theatre often relies on the fourth wall being intact: the characters behave as if they are unaware they are being watched. Brechtian theatre deliberately breaks the fourth wall — a performer steps forward, addresses the audience directly, and destroys the illusion, reminding them they are watching a performance.

Thrust Stage

A thrust stage pushes the performance area out into the auditorium so the audience wraps around three sides. This closes the physical distance between performer and audience and makes proxemics — the use of physical distance as a communicator — more acute: the audience can see the performer’s face and hands with far more detail than in a large proscenium house. A performer standing at the tip of the thrust, surrounded on three sides by the audience, is deeply exposed; there is no upstage safety. Blocking (the pattern of a performer’s movement around the stage) must be designed with all three audience sides in mind. The Elizabethan Globe Theatre used a thrust configuration, and Shakespeare’s plays were written for it.

Theatre in the round places the audience on all four sides. The performance area is typically a central square or circle, entered and exited through aisles between the audience blocks. This creates maximum intimacy — the audience feels they are in the room with the characters, not observing from outside — and maximum exposure for the performer. Every performer’s back is turned to some of the audience at any given moment, which means blocking and movement must keep the action alive and visible from all sides. Designers cannot use tall set pieces that block sightlines, and the lighting rig must light from all directions. In-the-round staging suits plays that explore raw human behaviour and want the audience to feel implicated rather than distanced.

Traverse staging (also called corridor staging) places two audience banks facing each other across a long, narrow performance space. The effect is that both audience groups can see each other across the action, creating a sense of surveillance or voyeurism. Performers travel down the “corridor” and their faces alternate between being visible and hidden to each audience group. This configuration suits plays about conflict, opposition, or social division — the geometry reinforces the idea of two sides watching each other across a contested space.

End-On Staging and Promenade

End-on staging is, in practice, very similar to a proscenium arch arrangement: the audience sits in front, the stage is a rectangle facing them. The difference is that there is no arch frame — the stage and audience share the same continuous space, which can create a slightly less formal, more immediate feel. Many studio or black box theatres are configured end-on because the space is flexible and the seats can be repositioned for a different production.

Promenade staging removes the fixed seating entirely. The audience follows the performers through a series of locations — corridors, rooms, outdoor spaces — or stands in an open space as the action moves around them. The audience becomes part of the physical world of the play. Their proximity is uncontrolled: a performer can address an individual directly, step up close, or move away to the far end of the space, leaving the audience to turn and find the action. Promenade productions require extremely careful stage management because sightlines cannot be guaranteed and the movement of the audience is a variable the director must plan for.

Key Fact

Stage positioning terminology — upstage left, upstage right, upstage centre, downstage left, downstage right, centre stage, stage left and stage right — is always given from the performer’s perspective, not the audience’s. Stage left is to the performer’s left as they face the audience. A performer standing downstage right (close to the audience, on the performer’s right) is at the most dominant position in a traditional proscenium staging, because it is the closest point to the majority of the audience and the eye naturally travels there.

The most common error is to confuse in-the-round (audience on all four sides) with thrust (audience on three sides), or to define a proscenium arch as simply “a normal theatre”. Another error is to forget that end-on is not proscenium — the proscenium arch configuration specifically requires the framing arch. Make sure you can define each configuration precisely, state how many sides of the audience are present, and name one implication for a performer or designer working in that space. The exam can ask you to choose a configuration for a specific dramatic purpose and justify your choice — so know not just what each configuration is, but what it does to the performer-audience relationship.
exam_tip_html: Questions about theatre configurations often ask you to “explain the effect” of a particular configuration on the audience or to “analyse the implications” for a designer or performer. A 4-mark answer needs to name the configuration, describe its defining feature (where the audience sits), and explain at least two implications — one for performer and one for designer, or two different effects on the audience relationship. For 8-mark or 20-mark questions where you must choose a configuration, commit to one and justify it: “I would stage this production as theatre in the round because the playwright intends the audience to feel implicated in the events, and the proximity of the in-the-round configuration removes the safety of observation that a proscenium arch provides.” Avoid hedging by describing multiple configurations without committing to one — it reads as uncertainty rather than analysis. Remember: stage left and stage right are always from the performer’s perspective, facing the audience.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The six staging configurations are proscenium arch, thrust, theatre in the round, traverse, end-on, and promenade. Each creates a distinct performer-audience relationship and has specific implications for blocking, sightlines and design.
  • Stage positioning terms (upstage, downstage, stage left, stage right, centre stage) are always from the performer's perspective facing the audience. Downstage is closest to the audience; upstage is furthest away.
  • The fourth wall is the imaginary barrier between the world of the play and the audience. Naturalistic theatre maintains it; Brechtian theatre deliberately breaks it through direct address.

practice_questions.text: In which staging configuration does the audience sit on all four sides of the performance space?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: theatre in the round.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'proxemics' in theatre?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that proxemics refers to physical distance on stage; 1 mark for explaining that it concerns the distances between performers, and between performers and audience, and how those distances communicate power, intimacy or relationship.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a thrust stage affects the performer's use of the performance space compared to a proscenium arch stage.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for correctly defining a thrust stage (performance area extends into the audience, audience on three sides); 1 mark for contrasting with proscenium (audience on one side only, frame separating stage and auditorium); 1 mark for explaining an implication for blocking (the performer must play to three sides; their back is always turned to some of the audience); 1 mark for explaining an implication for audience relationship (greater proximity, more visible physical detail, higher exposure for the performer).

practice_questions.text: Explain how staging a production in the round rather than using a proscenium arch might affect the audience's experience of the performance.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for defining theatre in the round (audience surrounds the space on all sides); 1 mark for identifying a specific effect on audience experience (e.g. the audience feels implicated or immersed rather than distanced; they can see each other watching across the space, which emphasises shared community or shared guilt); 1 mark for identifying a limitation or challenge (sightlines cannot be guaranteed; every performer's back is turned to part of the audience); 1 mark for analytical development (e.g. this configuration suits a play that wants the audience to feel unable to escape their role as witness).

practice_questions.text: As a set designer, explain how you would design a set for a traverse stage production. In your answer, discuss how the configuration affects your design choices and what effect your set would have on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: specific understanding of traverse configuration (two audience banks facing each other across a long narrow space); at least two specific set design choices driven by the configuration (e.g. low-profile furniture so sightlines are maintained; a minimal, symbolic central set piece such as a bare table and two chairs to emphasise the confrontational symmetry of the space; floor materials used to define zones rather than walls that would block views); each choice linked to a precise audience effect (e.g. 'the audience on both sides watches the other group watching the performers, which creates a sense that everyone is under surveillance'); scale, shape and texture referenced.

Secure: traverse configuration understood; at least two design choices described with some specificity; audience effect generally described.

Developing: configuration recognised but design choices are generic and not driven by traverse's specific demands; audience effect implied.

Emerging: basic staging ideas with no specific understanding of traverse; little or no discussion of how the configuration shapes the design.

practice_questions.text: As a designer, compare two staging configurations and explain which you would choose for a production exploring themes of surveillance, power and control. Justify your choice with reference to specific design and staging possibilities each configuration offers or denies.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: two configurations clearly defined and contrasted; the chosen configuration is justified with reference to the theme (surveillance, power, control) and at least two specific staging/design possibilities it enables (e.g. traverse: the audience watches the action across a contested space, seeing each other watching, which mirrors the theme of mutual observation; in-the-round: the performers are surrounded and cannot escape, embodying the theme of constant scrutiny); specific design choices discussed (set, lighting or sound elements that work with the chosen configuration); the rejected configuration is discussed to strengthen the argument.

Secure: two configurations compared; chosen configuration justified with theme in view; at least one specific staging/design possibility named per configuration; some design vocabulary used.

Developing: two configurations described but comparison is superficial; theme mentioned but not sustained in the argument; design choices general.

Emerging: one or two configurations named with basic description; no clear justification for choice; theme not connected to configuration.

knowledge_checks.q: Which staging configuration has the audience on three sides of the performance space?
Stage left and stage right are always given from whose perspective?
options: The director, watching from the auditorium
The stage manager, positioned in the wings

knowledge_checks.q: The _____ is an imaginary wall at the edge of the stage that separates the world of the play from the audience.
In a promenade production, the audience _____ through the performance space as the action takes place in multiple locations around them.
Match each staging configuration to its defining feature:
right: Audience on one side, separated from the stage by a rectangular frame
Audience surrounds the performance space on all four sides
Audience sits on two opposite sides with a narrow performance corridor between them

flashcard_questions.q: What is a proscenium arch stage configuration?
flashcard_questions.a: Audience on one side, viewing action through a rectangular frame that separates auditorium from stage.

flashcard_questions.q: How many sides of the audience are present in theatre in the round?
flashcard_questions.a: Four — the audience surrounds the performance space on all sides.
Performance area extends into the auditorium with audience on three sides.
Audience on two opposite sides with a long, narrow performance space between them.

flashcard_questions.q: In which direction is 'downstage' in stage positioning?
flashcard_questions.a: Towards the audience — the area of the stage closest to the spectators.

flashcard_questions.q: Stage right is to which side when standing on stage facing the audience?
flashcard_questions.a: The performer's right — which is the audience's left.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the fourth wall in theatre?
flashcard_questions.a: The imaginary barrier between the world of the play and the audience.
The use of physical distances between performers, and between performer and audience, to communicate meaning.
The audience moves through the space as the action takes place in multiple locations around them.

flashcard_questions.q: Which historical theatre used a thrust configuration that Shakespeare's plays were written for?
What is the key limitation of theatre in the round for performers?
flashcard_questions.a: Their back is always turned to part of the audience, so blocking must keep the action visible from all sides.

glossary_terms.definition: The arrangement of the performance space and audience seating that determines the relationship between performers and spectators throughout a production.
A stage configuration in which the audience sits on one side and views the action through a rectangular frame that separates the auditorium from the stage.
The area at the back of the stage, furthest from the audience.
The area of the stage closest to the audience.
An imaginary wall at the edge of the stage separating the world of the play from the audience; breaking it means directly acknowledging the audience's presence.
A stage configuration in which the performance area extends into the audience, with spectators on three sides.
The physical distances between performers on stage, and between performers and audience, which carry meaning about power, intimacy and relationship.
A staging configuration in which the audience surrounds the performance space on all four sides.
A staging configuration in which the audience sits on two opposite sides with the performance area running between them like a corridor.
A staging configuration in which the audience moves through the performance space and the action takes place in multiple locations around them.
